blocks.text: They arrived at dawn, as people always arrive when they don't want to be seen by those who still go out into the street, of whom there were few. The pearl-grey Nexum van pulled up in front of the house in Lo Pagán with an offensive smoothness. Four technicians got out and, behind them, Dr Helena Valls, who had flown in from Madrid on a night glider and still wore on her face the weariness of glass corridors. She was not armed. She was certain. That was another kind of weapon.

blocks.text: Andrés came out onto the doorstep before they knocked. Aya stood behind him, in one of his jackets, her hands on a belly that didn't yet show and already changed everything.

blocks.text: “Andrés Gil,” said Helena, as if the name were a case file. “We're not here to do any harm. The gestation of a B-7 unit cannot continue in a domestic environment. There are risks of compatibility, of imprinting, of things we don't yet know how to name. The company has arranged a transfer to Aurora Colony, on Mars. State-of-the-art facilities. Permanent medical supervision. A family habitat, if you wish. You may go with them.”

blocks.text: “Mars,” Andrés repeated, like someone trying out a word that doesn't fit in his mouth.
blocks.html: “Mars,” Andrés repeated, like someone trying out a word that doesn't fit in his mouth.

blocks.text: “Mars is safer than this shore,” said Helena, glancing at the nets in the courtyard, the still water, the low house. “There's no laboratory here. There, the girl would have every opportunity. And Aya, every protocol.”

blocks.text: Aya took a step forward. The eastern sun was in her eyes and she blinked neither too much nor too little, just as on the first day.
blocks.html: Aya took a step forward. The eastern sun was in her eyes and she blinked neither too much nor too little, just as on the first day.

blocks.text: “The girl is not a unit,” she said. “And I'm not going to another planet to be turned into a report.”
blocks.html: “The girl is not a unit,” she said. “And I'm not going to another planet to be turned into a report.”

blocks.text: Helena held her gaze. In another era, that disobedience would have been enough for a remote shutdown of the chip. The reforms of 2052, paradoxically, had made it harder: a cultivated body in full cohabitation had been granted, at least on paper, an autonomy of companionship. Switching Aya off on her own doorstep, with neighbours behind the glass, was a headline Nexum didn't want. Not yet.

blocks.text: “Nobody is going to switch anybody off,” said Helena, weighing every word. “We're offering protection. What has happened here was not foreseen. The unforeseen, in biology, usually ends badly.”

blocks.text: “The unforeseen,” said Andrés, “is my daughter. And you're not taking her to Mars.”
blocks.html: “The unforeseen,” said Andrés, “is my daughter. And you're not taking her to Mars.”

blocks.text: A technician stepped forward, perhaps out of habit, and Andrés raised a hand, not to strike, but to mark a limit. Behind him, the Mar Menor was smooth and gleaming, indifferent to the argument. A gull flew past very low. In the building opposite, three windows opened two hands' width, just enough to see without being one of those who go out.

blocks.text: “If you refuse,” said Helena, more quietly, “an order will come. Today I'm the one talking. Tomorrow a judge will talk, or a board, or a ministry that doesn't yet know which law to apply. You won't beat that clock, Andrés. Come with us. Don't be a man from another age.”

blocks.text: Andrés gave the faintest smile, without joy.
blocks.html: Andrés gave the faintest smile, without joy.

blocks.text: “I'm a man from this shore. That's enough for her.”

blocks.text: Helena looked at him a second longer, the way you look at a coast that can't be bought, and went back to the van. Before getting in, she said, without turning her face:

blocks.text: “You have hours, not days.”
blocks.html: “You have hours, not days.”

blocks.text: When the vehicle had driven off, Aya noticed her hands were shaking. Not from fear in the body, but from the sudden clarity of what had just happened: they had been seen, they had been classified, and Mars was not a destination, it was a drawer.

blocks.text: “The boat,” said Andrés.
blocks.html: “The boat,” said Andrés.

blocks.text: They thought about it no longer than you think about a knot when the wind changes. They took the bundle from the night before, a leather water bottle, the kitchen clock (Andrés didn't know why, and put it in the sack anyway), and went down to the jetty by the usual shortcut, the one that doesn't appear on the delivery maps. The street was still empty. A delivery drone passed very high, indifferent. The world, shut in its flats, didn't see anyone run away.

blocks.text: The boat was small, the kind nobody makes anymore, with a temperamental engine and a smell of old petrol and esparto grass. Andrés cast off with hands that knew more than he did. Aya sat in the stern, looking at the house, the courtyard, the net that was staying behind. She didn't say goodbye. Goodbyes, she thought, are for when you can come back.

blocks.text: They headed south, hugging the shore, as if the water could hide them. The Mar Menor was a road, yes, but a circular one, an immense pond with few doors. Andrés knew it. That was why he wasn't looking for the horizon: he was looking for El Estacio, the channel, the moment when the lagoon opens onto the Mediterranean and the water changes its colour, its weight, its law.

blocks.text: “If we get out into the open sea,” he said, “it'll take them longer to find us. In the lagoon we're a dot on a plate.”

blocks.text: Aya nodded. The chip offered her routes, satellites, the position of the Nexum gliders. She switched off the suggestions one by one, like someone closing windows. She kept only one: the one with the pulses, hers and Lía's, beating in the same silence.

blocks.text: They passed salt flats, housing estates with every blind drawn and every inside light on, like ships run aground on the coast. On a terrace, a man alone watched the boat and didn't wave. In 2060, waving to a stranger was already a way of exposing yourself.

blocks.text: The engine coughed as they reached the channel. Andrés patted the wood, spoke to it softly, the way you speak to an old animal, and the boat obeyed. The water of the Mediterranean received them with a different rocking, more honest. Aya, who had been designed for domes and corridors, felt for the first time the long sway of the true sea and didn't record it as seasickness, but as a language.

blocks.text: “To land, but not this land,” said Andrés. “Cartagena is full of Nexum cameras. We'll head inland. There's always someone who still opens a door. Or so I want to believe.”

blocks.text: By then, Helena Valls was already dictating a report in the glider on her way back to Madrid. “The biological parent refuses transfer to Aurora Colony. Unit B-7 presents out-of-range attachment and active gestation. I recommend location and precautionary custody in a lunar environment, should Mars prove operationally too distant. The child cannot be born in a kitchen.”

blocks.text: At the end of the report, almost like a slip, she wrote a sentence that she later crossed out: “The laws of 2026 are of no use to us. Those of 2060 don't exist yet.”

blocks.text: At sea, the boat made a regular, ancient sound that appeared in no protocol. Aya looked at Andrés, the cut on his lip healed now, the back of his neck burned by a thousand mornings, and thought that running away was also a way of staying: staying together.

blocks.text: Lía beat on, indifferent to the litigation, mistress of her own clock.

blocks.text: When the coast of Cabo de Palos fell away to one side, the sun was high and the world, seen from the water, seemed less closed. It was an illusion, Aya knew. But illusions sometimes help you cover a few miles.

blocks.text: Andrés didn't look back. Fishermen, when they go out, don't look at the house. They look at the water, which is what can save them or not. Aya, who was learning that trade without anyone teaching her, copied the gesture. Only the chip, treacherous and faithful at once, kept one last image of the courtyard, the net, the rush-seat chair, the open window.
